outputs.L1: An exemplary embodiment of the invention relates to a method for determining the hydraulic permeability of rocks in a subsurface region. The method comprises: measuring in situ and/or calculating at least one independent seismic velocity of rocks at different locations within the subsurface region; identifying at least one lithological unit within the subsurface region based on the measured seismic velocities; acquiring, for the at least one lithological unit, at least one rock sample from at least one location within the subsurface region; measuring the porosity and permeability of the rock sample as functions of stress; measuring and/or calculating at least one independent seismic velocity of the at least one rock sample as a function of stress; computing the stiff and compliant porosities of the at least one rock sample; computing numerical coefficients of a given analytical permeability model based on the stiff and compliant porosities; computing coefficients of a given analytical model describing an elastic-compliance characteristic of the rock based on the stiff and compliant porosities; computing the stiff and compliant porosities for a plurality of other locations within the subsurface region; and computing the permeability of rocks belonging to the at least one lithological unit at the at least one location and at the plurality of other locations within the subsurface region.
outputs.L2: An illustrative embodiment of the invention provides a method for evaluating the hydraulic permeability of rock within a subsurface region. The method includes measuring in situ and/or calculating at least one independent seismic velocity of the rock at multiple locations in the region. At least one lithological unit is then identified from the measured seismic velocities. For each identified lithological unit, at least one rock sample is collected from at least one location within the subsurface region. The sample’s porosity and permeability are measured as functions of stress, and at least one independent seismic velocity of the sample is measured and/or calculated as a function of stress. Stiff and compliant porosity values are derived for the sample and used to determine numerical coefficients for a specified analytical permeability model. These porosity values are also used to calculate coefficients for a specified analytical model describing the rock’s elastic-compliance behavior. Stiff and compliant porosities are subsequently calculated for a plurality of additional locations in the subsurface region. Finally, the permeability of rock associated with the identified lithological unit is calculated for both the location from which the sample was obtained and the plurality of other locations in the region.
outputs.L3:
The method characterizes subsurface rock properties by measuring or calculating independent seismic velocities at multiple locations within a subsurface region. These velocity data are then analyzed to identify and delineate distinct lithological units. Representative rock samples are obtained from selected locations within the identified units to provide calibration data.

For each sample, porosity, permeability, and independent seismic velocities are measured or calculated over a range of stress conditions. The resulting data are used to separate the total porosity into stiff and compliant components. These porosity components serve as inputs for determining coefficients in analytical models that describe rock permeability and elastic compliance.

Once calibrated, the analytical models are applied throughout each lithological unit. They are used to estimate stiff porosity, compliant porosity, and permeability both at the sampled locations and at additional locations where direct rock measurements are unavailable. In this way, the method integrates seismic observations, laboratory rock measurements, and analytical modeling to characterize the spatial distribution and stress dependence of key subsurface rock properties.
outputs.L4:
The method provides a systematic way to estimate subsurface rock permeability by integrating field-scale seismic observations with laboratory measurements made on representative rock samples. A lithological unit is first identified in the subsurface using available geological, petrophysical, or seismic information. One or more samples representative of that unit are then tested in the laboratory under a range of effective-stress conditions. At each stress level, sample porosity, permeability, and seismic velocity are measured so that changes in pore structure and fluid-flow capacity can be related to corresponding changes in elastic properties.

The laboratory results are interpreted by separating the total pore volume into stiff and compliant porosity. Stiff pores are relatively insensitive to changes in effective stress, whereas compliant pores, such as thin cracks and grain-boundary voids, close more readily as stress increases. Because compliant pores can strongly affect both seismic velocity and permeability, this distinction provides a physical basis for connecting elastic measurements to fluid-flow behavior. Analytical rock-physics and permeability models are calibrated using the measured stress-dependent data to determine the model parameters that best describe the sampled lithology.

In-situ seismic velocities measured at multiple subsurface locations are then introduced into the calibrated models. For each location, the observed velocity is used to infer the corresponding pore-state characteristics, including the relative contributions of stiff and compliant porosity under local stress conditions. The inferred pore structure is subsequently converted into an estimate of permeability using the laboratory-calibrated relationship among velocity, porosity, effective stress, and permeability.

By repeating this calculation wherever suitable seismic-velocity data are available within the identified lithological unit, permeability can be estimated at locations where no core or direct permeability measurement exists. The approach therefore extends a limited set of laboratory measurements to a much larger subsurface volume while retaining a link to the stress sensitivity and pore structure of the actual rock. The resulting permeability distribution may support reservoir characterization, groundwater assessment, geothermal evaluation, carbon-storage planning, and other applications requiring an understanding of subsurface fluid flow.
outputs.L5:
### An Exemplary Embodiment

An exemplary embodiment is an illustrative example of how an invention, system, or concept may be implemented. The term is commonly used in patents and technical documents to explain specific features, components, or processes without limiting the broader scope of the invention.

In an exemplary embodiment, a system may include several interconnected components configured to perform a particular function. The described arrangement serves as one possible implementation, while alternative configurations, materials, methods, or technologies may also be used. Certain elements can be modified, replaced, combined, or omitted depending on the intended application.

Accordingly, an exemplary embodiment should be understood as explanatory rather than restrictive. It provides practical guidance and demonstrates the principles of the disclosed concept while allowing for other embodiments that achieve similar results.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent-style exemplary embodiment describing a method for determining hydraulic permeability of subsurface rocks using seismic velocities, lithological classification, rock samples, stress-dependent porosity and permeability, and stiff/compliant porosity models.
counterfactuals.output:
### Exemplary Embodiment

[0001] In one exemplary embodiment, a computer-implemented method determines hydraulic permeability of a subsurface rock volume from seismic velocity data calibrated using lithological information and stress-dependent measurements performed on representative rock samples.

[0002] Seismic data are acquired for a subsurface region using surface seismic, borehole seismic, vertical seismic profiling, cross-well tomography, sonic logging, or a combination thereof. Compressional-wave velocity \(V_P\) and shear-wave velocity \(V_S\) are determined for a plurality of subsurface locations. Bulk density \(\rho_b\) may be measured or estimated from well logs, seismic inversion, mineral composition, and porosity data. Dynamic elastic moduli may be calculated according to:

\[
G_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\rho_b V_S^2
\]

and

\[
K_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\rho_b\left(V_P^2-\frac{4}{3}V_S^2\right),
\]

where \(G_{\mathrm{dyn}}\) is dynamic shear modulus and \(K_{\mathrm{dyn}}\) is dynamic bulk modulus.

[0003] Each subsurface location is assigned to a lithological class. The assignment may be based on one or more of mineralogical logs, gamma-ray response, elemental spectroscopy, core descriptions, cuttings, density, neutron porosity, seismic attributes, elastic moduli, and ratios such as \(V_P/V_S\). Exemplary lithological classes include sandstone, shale, carbonate, dolomite, chalk, siltstone, conglomerate, basement rock, and mixed or laminated lithologies. A probabilistic classifier may provide a probability that a location belongs to each of a plurality of classes rather than assigning only a single class.

[0004] One or more rock samples representative of each lithological class are obtained from cores, sidewall cores, outcrop analogues, or synthetically prepared analogues. Each sample is subjected to a plurality of confining pressures and, optionally, independently controlled pore pressures. Effective stress may be represented as:

\[
\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sigma_c-\alpha P_p,
\]

where \(\sigma_c\) is confining stress, \(P_p\) is pore pressure, and \(\alpha\) is a Biot coefficient or an empirically determined effective-stress coefficient.

[0005] At each of a plurality of effective stresses, the sample is characterized to determine porosity, compressional-wave velocity, shear-wave velocity, and hydraulic permeability. Permeability may be measured using steady-state flow, pulse-decay, pressure-transient, or oscillatory-flow testing. Measurements may be conducted using a formation-representative fluid and at formation-representative temperature. Loading and unloading measurements may be obtained to identify hysteresis or irreversible pore collapse.

[0006] The total connected porosity \(\phi\) of a sample is represented as including stiff porosity and compliant porosity:

\[
\phi(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})=\phi_s(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})+\phi_c(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}).
\]

Stiff porosity \(\phi_s\) corresponds primarily to approximately equant pores or pore bodies having relatively low stress sensitivity. Compliant porosity \(\phi_c\) corresponds primarily to cracks, grain-boundary openings, narrow pore throats, and high-aspect-ratio voids having greater stress sensitivity.

[0007] In one implementation, the stress dependence of the porosity components is expressed as:

\[
\phi_s(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})
=
\phi_{s0}\exp(-c_s\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})
\]

and

\[
\phi_c(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})
=
\phi_{c0}\exp(-c_c\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}}),
\]

where \(\phi_{s0}\) and \(\phi_{c0}\) are reference stiff and compliant porosities, respectively, and \(c_c>c_s\). Other compaction laws, including linear, power-law, hyperbolic, or piecewise functions, may be used.

[0008] The elastic response of each sample is fitted with a rock-physics model that separately accounts for stiff and compliant porosity. For example, a mineral-frame modulus may be determined from mineral fractions, after which stiff porosity is incorporated using an effective-medium model and compliant porosity is incorporated using a crack-compliance model. Fluid substitution may be performed to account for differences between laboratory and in-situ pore fluids. The fitted model establishes a lithology-specific relationship of the form:

\[
(V_P,V_S,\rho_b,\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}},S_f)
\longrightarrow
(\phi_s,\phi_c),
\]

where \(S_f\) represents one or more fluid-state parameters, such as saturation, fluid bulk modulus, viscosity, and pore pressure.

[0009] A stress-dependent permeability model is fitted for each lithological class using the laboratory measurements. In one example, permeability is represented by:

\[
k(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})
=
k_{\mathrm{ref}}
\left(
\frac{\phi_s(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})}{\phi_{s,\mathrm{ref}}}
\right)^{m}
\left(
\frac{\phi_c(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})}{\phi_{c,\mathrm{ref}}}
\right)^{n},
\]

where \(k_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is a reference permeability and \(m\) and \(n\) are calibrated exponents. The exponent \(n\) may be greater than \(m\) where permeability is controlled principally by stress-sensitive cracks or pore throats.

[0010] In another implementation, the permeability model includes separate stiff-pore and compliant-pore flow contributions:

\[
k(\sigma_{\mathrm{eff}})
=
k_s\left(\phi_s\right)
+
k_c\left(\phi_c\right),
\]

or a connectivity-weighted combination thereof. A percolation or threshold term may be included so that the compliant-pore contribution decreases sharply when \(\phi_c\) falls below a lithology-dependent connectivity threshold. Tortuosity, specific surface area, grain size, clay content, cementation, pore-throat radius, and anisotropy may also be included as model parameters.

[0011] At an in-situ subsurface location, overburden stress, horizontal stress, and pore pressure are obtained or estimated to determine effective stress. The measured seismic velocities are corrected, when appropriate, for anisotropy, dispersion, attenuation, frequency-dependent fluid effects, temperature, and the difference between dynamic and static elastic response. The corrected velocities and density are supplied to the rock-physics model associated with the assigned lithological class.

[0012] The model is inverted to estimate stiff porosity and compliant porosity at the in-situ effective stress. In one implementation, estimated values minimize an objective function:

\[
J=
w_P\left(V_P^{\mathrm{obs}}-V_P^{\mathrm{mod}}\right)^2+
w_S\left(V_S^{\mathrm{obs}}-V_S^{\mathrm{mod}}\right)^2+
w_\rho\left(\rho_b^{\mathrm{obs}}-\rho_b^{\mathrm{mod}}\right)^2+
R,
\]

where \(w_P\), \(w_S\), and \(w_\rho\) are weighting factors and \(R\) is a regularization term constraining porosity, stress sensitivity, spatial continuity, or lithology. Bayesian inversion may alternatively be used to generate posterior probability distributions for \(\phi_s\) and \(\phi_c\).

[0013] The estimated stiff and compliant porosities are applied to the calibrated permeability model to calculate hydraulic permeability at each subsurface location. The resulting permeability may be expressed as intrinsic permeability, liquid permeability, gas permeability, or directional permeability. Where the rock is anisotropic, separate components \(k_x\), \(k_y\), and \(k_z\), or a permeability tensor, may be determined using direction-dependent velocities and sample measurements made parallel and perpendicular to bedding, fractures, or principal stress directions.

[0014] When lithological classification is probabilistic, permeability may be calculated for each candidate lithology and combined according to:

\[
\bar{k}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N} P(L_i\mid D)\,k_i,
\]

where \(P(L_i\mid D)\) is the probability of lithological class \(L_i\) given input data \(D\), and \(k_i\) is the permeability estimated using the model for class \(L_i\). Confidence intervals may additionally account for uncertainty in velocity, density, stress, pore pressure, fluid properties, and sample calibration parameters.

[0015] The calculated permeability values are assembled into a one-, two-, or three-dimensional permeability representation of the subsurface region. The representation may be used for reservoir simulation, groundwater assessment, geothermal development, carbon dioxide sequestration, underground gas storage, hydrocarbon production, well placement, stimulation design, or prediction of permeability changes caused by depletion, injection, or changes in effective stress.

[0016] In a further aspect, the method predicts time-dependent permeability by updating pore pressure and effective stress during a production or injection simulation, recalculating the compliant and stiff porosity components, and updating permeability. Thus, the method accounts for permeability reduction caused by closure of compliant pores and for permeability recovery or hysteresis during unloading.

[0017] The foregoing operations may be performed by one or more processors executing instructions stored in non-transitory computer-readable memory. The processors may receive seismic, logging, laboratory, geological, and stress data; select or train lithology-specific rock-physics and permeability models; perform the inversion; and output permeability values, uncertainty measures, and spatial permeability maps.

A method for estimating rock permeability throughout a subsurface region, the method comprising: acquiring in-situ seismic measurements at a plurality of locations within the subsurface region; obtaining representative rock samples corresponding to one or more rock types present in the subsurface region; measuring, under laboratory conditions, permeability and at least one seismic-response property of each representative rock sample; deriving a calibration relationship between the measured permeability and the at least one seismic-response property while accounting for differences between the laboratory conditions and in-situ conditions; determining, from the in-situ seismic measurements, spatially distributed values of the at least one seismic-response property throughout the subsurface region; and applying the calibration relationship to the spatially distributed values to generate a spatial estimate of rock permeability throughout the subsurface region.

counterfactuals.prompt: Formulate an invention embodiment that combines seismic velocity data, lithological units, stress-dependent core analysis, elastic-compliance modeling, and analytical permeability coefficients to predict permeability at sampled and unsampled locations.
counterfactuals.output:
### Exemplary Invention Embodiment

In one embodiment, a computer-implemented method predicts formation permeability at both sampled and unsampled subsurface locations by integrating seismic velocity data, lithological classification, stress-dependent core measurements, elastic-compliance modeling, and analytically determined permeability coefficients.

1. **Seismic and lithological model generation**  
   Compressional-wave velocity \(V_P\), shear-wave velocity \(V_S\), and, when available, density \(\rho\) are obtained from seismic inversion, sonic logs, or vertical seismic profiles. Each subsurface cell is assigned either a lithological unit \(L\) or a set of lithological probabilities \(P(L)\) using well logs, core descriptions, seismic attributes, or a geostatistical earth model.

2. **Elastic-compliance calculation**  
   Dynamic elastic moduli are calculated from the velocity data, for example:

   \[
   G_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\rho V_S^2,
   \qquad
   K_{\mathrm{dyn}}=\rho\left(V_P^2-\frac{4}{3}V_S^2\right).
   \]

   The corresponding dynamic compliance tensor or selected normal and shear compliance components are then determined. Lithology-specific correction functions convert the dynamic compliance to static, stress-dependent compliance:

   \[
   \mathbf S_L(\sigma')
   =
   \mathcal C_L\!\left(\mathbf S_{\mathrm{dyn}},\sigma'\right),
   \]

   where \(\sigma'\) is effective stress and \(\mathcal C_L\) is calibrated separately for each lithological unit.

3. **Stress-dependent core calibration**  
   Core plugs representing the lithological units are tested at multiple confining pressures and pore pressures. Permeability, porosity, axial strain, radial strain, and ultrasonic velocity are measured at each effective-stress state. The measurements establish lithology-specific relationships among effective stress, elastic compliance, pore or fracture closure, and permeability. Directional core tests may be used to characterize anisotropic compliance and permeability tensors.

4. **Analytical permeability coefficients**  
   For each lithological unit, permeability is represented by an analytical expression such as:

   \[
   \ln k_{i,L}
   =
   a_{i,L}
   +b_{i,L}\phi
   +c_{i,L}S_N
   +d_{i,L}S_T
   +e_{i,L}\sigma'
   +f_{i,L}\sigma' S_N,
   \]

   where \(k_{i,L}\) is permeability in direction \(i\), \(\phi\) is porosity, \(S_N\) and \(S_T\) are selected normal and shear compliance measures, and \(a\) through \(f\) are lithology-dependent permeability coefficients.

   The coefficient vector may be calculated directly by a regularized analytical estimator:

   \[
   \boldsymbol\beta_L
   =
   \left(\mathbf X_L^\mathsf{T}\mathbf W_L\mathbf X_L+\lambda\mathbf I\right)^{-1}
   \mathbf X_L^\mathsf{T}\mathbf W_L\mathbf y_L,
   \]

   where \(\mathbf y_L\) contains measured logarithmic core permeabilities, \(\mathbf X_L\) contains the corresponding porosity, compliance, and stress terms, and \(\mathbf W_L\) weights measurements according to uncertainty or representativeness.

5. **Prediction at sampled locations**  
   At a cored or logged location, the measured lithology, local effective stress, core-calibrated compliance, and available porosity are supplied to the analytical expression. The resulting permeability is compared with measured permeability, and residuals are used to update the lithology-specific correction functions or coefficients.

6. **Prediction at unsampled locations**  
   For each unsampled cell, the system obtains seismic-derived \(V_P\), \(V_S\), and density; determines dynamic compliance; applies the lithology-specific static and stress correction; estimates effective stress from overburden pressure, pore pressure, and structural orientation; and evaluates the analytical permeability expression. Where lithology is probabilistic, the predicted permeability may be calculated as:

   \[
   \hat{k}_i(\mathbf x)
   =
   \sum_L P(L\mid\mathbf x)\,
   \exp\!\left(\mathbf X_L(\mathbf x)\boldsymbol\beta_L\right).
   \]

7. **Output**  
   The system generates a three-dimensional scalar permeability volume or anisotropic permeability tensor field, together with confidence intervals derived from seismic uncertainty, lithological probability, stress uncertainty, and coefficient covariance. The permeability field may be updated for different depletion, injection, or geomechanical scenarios by changing the effective-stress field without repeating the core-calibration procedure.

The embodiment thereby uses stress-sensitive core behavior to translate seismic-scale elastic response into lithology-conditioned permeability estimates, permitting consistent predictions where direct permeability samples are unavailable.

counterfactuals.output: A method comprising: obtaining, for a subsurface rock volume, independent measurements of compressional-wave velocity and shear-wave velocity; determining mineralogical composition, fluid properties, pressure, temperature, density, and total porosity associated with the subsurface rock volume; obtaining laboratory measurements from representative rock samples under a plurality of effective-stress conditions; deriving from the laboratory measurements a stiff-porosity relationship that relates a first portion of pore volume carried by relatively high-aspect-ratio or load-bearing pores to seismic velocity, and a compliant-porosity relationship that relates a second portion of pore volume carried by relatively low-aspect-ratio pores, cracks, or stress-sensitive voids to seismic velocity; constructing a rock-physics model that independently predicts compressional-wave velocity and shear-wave velocity as functions of stiff porosity, compliant porosity, mineral moduli, pore-fluid moduli, density, and effective stress; jointly inverting the independent compressional-wave and shear-wave velocity measurements using the rock-physics model and the laboratory-derived stiff-porosity and compliant-porosity relationships to determine respective stiff-porosity and compliant-porosity values for the subsurface rock volume, subject to a constraint that a sum of the stiff-porosity and compliant-porosity values is consistent with the total porosity; calculating a hydraulically effective porosity, pore-throat parameter, connectivity parameter, or combination thereof by weighting the stiff-porosity and compliant-porosity values according to laboratory-determined contributions to fluid flow; calculating hydraulic permeability of the subsurface rock volume by applying a laboratory-calibrated permeability relationship to the hydraulically effective porosity, pore-throat parameter, connectivity parameter, effective stress, or combination thereof; validating or updating the calculated hydraulic permeability using one or more core-permeability, pressure-transient, formation-tester, production, or injection measurements; and generating, storing, or displaying a depth-dependent or spatially distributed estimate of hydraulic permeability for use in well placement, reservoir characterization, stimulation design, fluid-flow simulation, or production forecasting.
